title: Latency Start Timestamp Misplaced Around Serialization and Send
pattern: The start timestamp of a request-latency measurement is placed on the wrong side of the send: before CPU-heavy client work such as serialization, formatting or large allocations, or after `write`/`send` returns, so the measured interval does not match the network/server round trip it is reported as.
why_bad: Starting too early mixes client CPU and allocator noise into the server/network latency distribution. Starting after the write excludes time spent blocked in `write_all` when socket send buffers are full, which is exactly the queueing that grows under load, so latency looks flat while the system saturates.
detection: Between `Instant::now()` and the socket write: serialization (`serde_json::to_vec`, `format!`, encoding) or large buffer construction. Or an `Instant::now()` placed after a `write`/`write_all`/`send` call and before the matching `read`/`recv`, with the result reported as request latency.
counterexample: End-to-end client SDK benchmarks where serialization is part of the declared client-overhead budget, and benchmarks explicitly isolating server turnaround on established connections (`T3 - T2`), labelled as such.
source: Richard L. Sites, *Understanding Software Dynamics* (2021), Ch. 1, §1.4, p. 7; Ch. 13, §13.7, p. 215; Ch. 26, §26.5, p. 323.
